article_text:
With the major fall auctions right around the corner, ARTnews can reveal that the consignor of Betonte Ecken (1922–23), the Wassily Kandinsky painting set to achieve upwards of $60M at Christie’s New York on November 17, is the Nahmad family.

The Nahmads are a prominent dynasty of dealers and collectors whose holdings are reputed to include as many as 5,000 artworks worth upwards of $4 billion. The family is also known to be the largest private collector of works by Pablo Picasso outside the Picasso family itself.

Several exhibition catalogs from the past 25 years have listed the Nahmad Collection as the owner of Betonte Ecken . Among them are Art of Tomorrow: Hilla Rebay and Solomon R. Guggenheim (2005) and Geometric Abstraction in the Twentieth Century: Kandinsky’s Universe (2025), produced by the Museum Barberini in Potsdam, Germany.

With an estimate of $60 million to $80 million, the Kandinsky is the highest-priced lot in Christie’s November sales. The work carries a third party guarantee that, according to the auction house, ensures that it will break the artist’s auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II, 1910) at Sotheby’s London in 2023.

The colorful abstraction measures just over four feet square. Kandinsky painted it in Weimar, Germany, while he was teaching at the legendary Bauhaus.

As ARTnews ’s Brian Boucher reported last week:

The painting has changed hands a number of times. Christie’s provenance shows it first coming to auction at the Jacob Hecht Auction House in Berlin in 1926, from the Schwarz collection, going to that city’s Galerie Nierendorf, which then sold it, probably in 1929, to Hilla Rebay—adviser to museum founder Solomon R. Guggenheim, an early supporter of abstract art in the US. Guggenheim later acquired it from Rebay, and it remained in the museum’s collection until 1964, when the museum sold it at Sotheby’s London to New York art dealer Stephen Hahn. At some point, Hahn sold it to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar, who put it up for auction at Sotheby’s in 1986, when it went to the present owner.

That present owner, it seems, is the Nahmad family. Christie’s declined a request to comment. The Nahmads did not respond by press time.

article_text:
John Leguizamo , Indya Moore and D’Arcy Carden will be honored at the 49th Denver Film Festival , which runs Oct. 22—Nov. 1.

Leguizamo will receive the John Cassavetes Award presented by Next50. The actor will make an appearance at the festival on Oct. 30 to accept the honor prior to a newly added screening of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” in which Leguizamo starred as Eumaeus.

Related Stories

Marjoe Gortner, Preacher and Actor Who Was Subject of Oscar-Winning Doc and Appeared in 'Earthquake,' 'Falcon Crest,' Dies at 82

Bernie Orenstein, Co-Writer of 'That Girl' and 'The New Dick Van Dyke Show,' Dies at 95

Indya Moore will receive the CinemaQ LaBahn Ikon Award at the Denver Art Museum on Oct. 25. The actress, model, writer and producer — known for her role as Angel on FX’s “Pose” — will participate in a moderated conversation with Jill D’Allessandro, curator for the museum’s “DIVA” exhibit, which runs Oct. 4—Jan. 31, 2027.

D’Arcy Carden (“The Good Place, “The Five-Star Weekend”) will receive the Women+Film Barbara Bridges Inspiration Award at the Festival’s Awards Brunch on Nov. 1.

Popular on Variety

“We couldn’t be more excited to welcome three extraordinary artists whose talent, creativity and impact extend far beyond the screen,” said Matthew Campbell, Denver Film Festival artistic director. “John Leguizamo has built a remarkable career defined by fearless performances, incredible range and the independent spirit that makes him such a deserving recipient of our Cassavetes Award. Indya Moore is a groundbreaking artist and powerful voice for representation and inclusion, while D’Arcy Carden brings an exceptional combination of comedic brilliance, versatility and heart to everything she does. Each has made a unique and lasting mark on the entertainment industry, and we’re thrilled to celebrate their achievements and give Denver audiences the opportunity to connect with these inspiring artists during this year’s Festival.”

The DFF program will also include six Creative Conversations with filmmakers and industry experts. The discussions will be held in the lower level of The Tattered Cover and include:

Screenwriting with Peter Gamble — Oct. 23 at 11:30 a.m. Peter Gamble screenwriter, “I Play Rocky”

When the Buses Arrived — Oct. 27 at 11 a.m. Al Jackson, moderator Andrea Ryall, founder, Hope Has No Borders Karen Orona, communications manager at the Colorado Immigrants’ Rights Coalition Jon Ewing, press secretary for the Denver Mayor’s Office Rebekah Henderson and Lilah Park, filmmakers

Muddy Waters – Navigating the Colorado River’s Uncertain Future — Oct. 27 at 1 p.m. Tahlia Bear, moderator Mara Tasker, director, “The River” Lorelei Cloud, film participant and water activist Jim Lochhead, former CEO of Denver Water Perry Cabot, CSU Extension professor and water expert

The Evolving Television Landscape, presented by SeriesFest — Oct. 29, 12:30 p.m. John Wenzel, moderator and Denver Post journalist Teri Weinberg, president, Yellow Brick Road Alex Maggioni, head of television at LAIKA Live Action Elsie Choi, founder and executive producer, Hours and Seasons

Costume Design with Mona May — Oct. 30, 11 a.m. Mona May, costume designer, “Clueless”

Casting Director Karlee Formalont — Oct. 30, 1 p.m. Karlee Formalont, casting director, “A Complete Unknown,” “The Post”

DFF49 will also screen and judge selected films in competition. Jurors for this year’s in-competitions films include:

Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film David Canfield, The Hollywood Reporter Destiny Jackson, Deadline Rochelle Rose, national director, Performers Program, SAG-AFTRA Foundation

Maysles Brothers Award for Best Documentary Justine Suzanne Jones, producer Ryan Lattanzio, IndieWire Chris Murphy, Vanity Fair

True Grit Award Ethan Alter, Gold Derby Karlee Fomalont, casting director Danielle Rose Russell, actress

Shorts Competitions Kate Chamuris, producer Mona May, costume designer Darwin Shaw, producer

article_text:
Gallerie d’Italia in Milan presents “LIBERE! 1946–2026. Le conquiste delle donne” ( FREE! 1946–2026. Women’s Hard-Won Rights) , an exhibition curated by Renata Ferri that traces almost eighty years of women’s achievements in Italy, beginning with the vote of June 2, 1946.

By Gaia Squarci. Cover Photo by Publifoto Archive, Intesa Sanpaolo

Through photographs from Italy’s major historical archives, the exhibition traces the social and cultural changes that led women toward emancipation. Running through the whole show is a tension between work and leisure, independence and tradition, captured in scenes of factory workers after World War II, office clerks of the economic boom, housewives, women casting their first votes, and girls screaming at a Beatles concert.

Then the focus shifts to the feminist movement and the battles over divorce and abortion, along with a tribute to women who left their mark on Italian culture, science, politics and the arts.

The final section brings together photographs and multimedia works by contemporary women artists. Above all, the show makes clear that rights are never handed out. They were won by earlier generations who fought for them, and they can be lost again at any time.

The exhibition “LIBERE! 1946–2026. Le conquiste delle donne” is on view at Gallerie d’Italia in Milan, Italy, until February 7, 2027.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ever since the first trailer went up for “ You Can See Everything ,” if not since word of the movie got up, schadenfreude lovers have been rubbing their hands with glee at the prospect of Elizabeth Holmes getting more of what’s coming to her. Especially knowing that Holmes and her husband Billy Evans actually sought out Nathan Fielder , who exudes a natural skepticism, to make the documentary, there’s been an anticipatory bloodlust, that they must have been fools to imagine they were doing anything but helping set their own trap. That’s not a completely ill-founded expectation: Holmes comes off in the doc as every bit as innately bizarre as anyone showing up for a cinematic freak show might hope. But the weirdest thing about the movie might be the fact that it at least allows for the possibility that the Evil Genius might be neither of the things contained in that descriptor, but rather somebody whose guileless act may not be that much of a put-on, because she’s dealing with some kind of mysterious damage we can only begin to guess at.", "links": [{"text": "You Can See Everything", "url": "https://variety.com/t/you-can-see-everything/"}, {"text": "Elizabeth Holmes", "url": "https://variety.com/t/elizabeth-holmes/"}, {"text": "Nathan Fielder", "url": "https://variety.com/t/nathan-fielder/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In other words, it’s a movie with some sympathy for the devil, or at least — given the admitted inconclusiveness of its findings — the suggestion that empathy may be possible. Which may be not what you’re expecting walking in to what looks like a hilarious 174-minute takedown. But the intentions of Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim , are embedded right in that first trailer that set the watching world ablaze. At the scene’s very end, when after a couple of minutes of Holmes smiling and staring earnestly into the narrator’s eyes, with a shaky head that makes it appear as if she’s developed some kind of anxious palsy, it’s revealed that she’s extending her left leg well off the couch to rock her baby. If you were watching that teaser carefully, the filmmakers were carefully signaling the whole movie: vast amounts of IRL comedic shock and awe, tinged with lingering bits of poignance as Holmes turns out to be a human being… if a still-unfathomable one.", "links": [{"text": "Lance Oppenheim", "url": "https://variety.com/t/lance-oppenheim/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So, let’s set a countdown for how long it takes for some souls on social media to begin calling Fielder a “cuck,” for having fallen prey to the manipulation of an obvious villain. But it’s not a movie that means to let Holmes off any hooks, only to ask some questions about where some of the invisible hooks in her impossibly strange life might lie. It’s a film that starts off with the intent to provide insight into a Leonard Nimoy- or Robert Stack-style unsolved-mystery episode, with the idea that spending 34 days living with Holmes and Evans — and years of further production beyond her incarceration — would surely have to provide a few concrete conclusions about her psychology and/or crimes. Instead, by the end, it makes solving the puzzle of UFOs seem like a cinch by comparison. Abnormal psychology: it’s the Ultimate Trip! But the idea that, amid that inability to form answers, we could at least further consider what makes her tick will seem risible and outrageous to some viewers… and is also what makes the film rich and re-visitable enough to deserve the Best Picture nomination it’s clearly lined up to get."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If there’s a great crux moment for the movie, it’s in the scene fairly late in the three-hour proceedings that involve a sort of postmortem between Fielder and the Very Famous A-List Personality whose appearance A24 has asked viewers to consider a spoiler. (Her name will be ubiquitous enough in the weeks to come, but we can honor the surprise for now.) Fielder confesses how confused he is, after spending months doing intensive filming of Holmes and her husband and immediate family — basically wondering if, against all odds, it is possible that she could be as guileless as she comes off 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Upon hearing that confession, the Very Famous A-List Personality does everything but literally slap Fielder, suggesting that he must be experiencing some kind of Stockholm Syndrome to have been pulled in by her act. At this, some filmgoers will be practically standing up and cheering for the A-lister — she has at that moment become the audience’s surrogate, or stand-in for at least part of it, urging the host/filmmaker to snap out of his delirium. But it won’t just be different viewers taking sides in this scene. It may be anyone watching the movie whose empathic and cynical sides are in roughly equal balance."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where Fielder ultimately ended up on the issue of how sincere or Machiavellian Holmes is another unsolved mystery at the end of the movie, perhaps even to himself. When I caught the film at its Telluride Film Festival premiere (followed by a Q&A attendees weren’t allowed to record), Fielder basically said that he and others on the filmmaking team still had trouble figuring out exactly what they’d experienced in the process of making the movie — which is a fascinating conundrum, considering that, true to its title, Holmes and her husband did let them see just about everything it seemed possible to see. My personal hunch is that Fielder came away thinking Holmes is on the level, to the extent that someone who sometimes seems like an AI program’s idea of how a human should behave can be on the level. There are a few possibilities that might explain how Holmes comes off the way she does in the movie: (a) She is a simpleton. (b) She is a conniving sociopath who happens to be utterly brilliant at playing a simpleton. (c) Somewhere between those poles, she is the very emblem of a woman who throughout her life has put herself in the sway of controlling men, to the detriment of her intellect, willpower and emotional development."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And what about those impossibly wide, unblinking eyes, and that gentle Joker smile? Are these the hallmarks, as I’ve seen theorized throughout the internet, of someone who is deeply sociopathic at worst, or on the scale at best? Or just someone with Resting Beatific Face?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The sort of feminist lens is a powerful one, if you choose to go down that path of interpretation. Fielder and Oppenheim include a moment early in the film in which Holmes’ father blurts out that he believes things really started to change for his daughter when she was raped in her college days. On-camera, Fielder offers one of the quietly startled reaction shots that are a staple of the movie, and the topic never comes up again. The theme of her becoming the victim of powerful men continues — a little bit when the subject of Theranos co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani comes up (although recounting past history doesn’t take up much of this doc’s running time), and a lot when we get to the present day. Evans is as close as “You Can See Everything” has to a villain, and probably crosses the line into counting as one. Even he is treated as a rounded human being over the course of the film; he’s too candid and open about ihs intentions to count as a top-level devil, and it seems like he might actually love Holmes. But the succession of constant revelations about what he’s up to in the last hour of the movie make Holmes feel like a woman with virtually no personal agency, even before she goes to jail, let alone afterward, when he is making deals without her knowledge and keeping up a cocky, profane tweetstorm under her name that bears scant resemblance to her personality as we know it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It may be not giving Holmes nearly enough credit for her misdeeds to suggest that she has actually spent most of her adult years as a puppet. Yet the portrait of her passivity in the face of an aggressive “let me handle everything” man never stops growing more startling as the film goes on… and has to feel at least a little real for anyone with much first-hand human-race experience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Two scenes that explore Holmes’ seeming — and shocking — naivete stand out. (Neither of these count as major “plot” spoilers.) One comes early on when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied, and when she says no, he asks the inevitable what-about-white-lies question. Even then, it’s a no, as Fielder almost begs her to admit that she understands the question and has told a fib or two to protect a friend’s feelings. Probably 99.99% of the population would surrender at the point — evil geniuses most of all — but Holmes can’t admit to even having falsely complimented a pal. Later on, there’s a mind-blowing scene in which Fielder uses the historically famous Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” sketch as a setup to explore how people’s communication paths might just blow right by each other. Holmes hasn’t heard of the skit, but after watching it, she says she sees what he’s trying to say… which itself turns out to be a white lie, because she finally admits that she just doesn’t get what’s going on between Abbott and Costello, at all . And it’s at this point that you might start to wonder if she is just developmentally disabled in some way."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Stunted in her growth, somehow, yet capable of convincing smart people to part with billions of dollars? Something here does not compute. And yet, intuitively, Holmes does not come off in this movie as someone with the kind of intellectual cunning to pretend not to understand an Abbott and Costello sketch that has entertained millions, or to not know what a white lie is. The enigma deepens."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But so does the possibility that, for all her sins, and for all her Stanford education, Holmes is a simple gal — not simpleton — suffering from an extreme case of not just serial male dominance but terminal Imposters’ Syndrome. (Which is something that, from the available evidence in the movie, she surely would not admit to, not least of all because she might never have heard of it.)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How people feel about Holmes after watching “You Can See Everything” might be the most divisive thing in America since… well, since Kelly Clarkson versus the Brooklyn boutique, the thing that has truly riven us as a nation. But one thing is clear: In this era of ever-shortening quick hits and hot takes, Fielder and Oppenheim’s luxuriously paced peering into someone’s soul feels like a balm, inconclusive or not. Is it possible that the more you learn about someone, the less you might know how to think about them?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To take a cue from Shakespeare: “You Can See Everything” suggests that there are more things in the heaven and earth that is just one person than are dreamt of in any of our philosophies. We could do worse than to have the possibility of sympathy thrown in amid those hours of head-scratching assessment."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "(By the way, who is on first…)"}]

Ever since the first trailer went up for “ You Can See Everything ,” if not since word of the movie got up, schadenfreude lovers have been rubbing their hands with glee at the prospect of Elizabeth Holmes getting more of what’s coming to her. Especially knowing that Holmes and her husband Billy Evans actually sought out Nathan Fielder , who exudes a natural skepticism, to make the documentary, there’s been an anticipatory bloodlust, that they must have been fools to imagine they were doing anything but helping set their own trap. That’s not a completely ill-founded expectation: Holmes comes off in the doc as every bit as innately bizarre as anyone showing up for a cinematic freak show might hope. But the weirdest thing about the movie might be the fact that it at least allows for the possibility that the Evil Genius might be neither of the things contained in that descriptor, but rather somebody whose guileless act may not be that much of a put-on, because she’s dealing with some kind of mysterious damage we can only begin to guess at.

In other words, it’s a movie with some sympathy for the devil, or at least — given the admitted inconclusiveness of its findings — the suggestion that empathy may be possible. Which may be not what you’re expecting walking in to what looks like a hilarious 174-minute takedown. But the intentions of Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim , are embedded right in that first trailer that set the watching world ablaze. At the scene’s very end, when after a couple of minutes of Holmes smiling and staring earnestly into the narrator’s eyes, with a shaky head that makes it appear as if she’s developed some kind of anxious palsy, it’s revealed that she’s extending her left leg well off the couch to rock her baby. If you were watching that teaser carefully, the filmmakers were carefully signaling the whole movie: vast amounts of IRL comedic shock and awe, tinged with lingering bits of poignance as Holmes turns out to be a human being… if a still-unfathomable one.

So, let’s set a countdown for how long it takes for some souls on social media to begin calling Fielder a “cuck,” for having fallen prey to the manipulation of an obvious villain. But it’s not a movie that means to let Holmes off any hooks, only to ask some questions about where some of the invisible hooks in her impossibly strange life might lie. It’s a film that starts off with the intent to provide insight into a Leonard Nimoy- or Robert Stack-style unsolved-mystery episode, with the idea that spending 34 days living with Holmes and Evans — and years of further production beyond her incarceration — would surely have to provide a few concrete conclusions about her psychology and/or crimes. Instead, by the end, it makes solving the puzzle of UFOs seem like a cinch by comparison. Abnormal psychology: it’s the Ultimate Trip! But the idea that, amid that inability to form answers, we could at least further consider what makes her tick will seem risible and outrageous to some viewers… and is also what makes the film rich and re-visitable enough to deserve the Best Picture nomination it’s clearly lined up to get.

If there’s a great crux moment for the movie, it’s in the scene fairly late in the three-hour proceedings that involve a sort of postmortem between Fielder and the Very Famous A-List Personality whose appearance A24 has asked viewers to consider a spoiler. (Her name will be ubiquitous enough in the weeks to come, but we can honor the surprise for now.) Fielder confesses how confused he is, after spending months doing intensive filming of Holmes and her husband and immediate family — basically wondering if, against all odds, it is possible that she could be as guileless as she comes off 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Upon hearing that confession, the Very Famous A-List Personality does everything but literally slap Fielder, suggesting that he must be experiencing some kind of Stockholm Syndrome to have been pulled in by her act. At this, some filmgoers will be practically standing up and cheering for the A-lister — she has at that moment become the audience’s surrogate, or stand-in for at least part of it, urging the host/filmmaker to snap out of his delirium. But it won’t just be different viewers taking sides in this scene. It may be anyone watching the movie whose empathic and cynical sides are in roughly equal balance.

Where Fielder ultimately ended up on the issue of how sincere or Machiavellian Holmes is another unsolved mystery at the end of the movie, perhaps even to himself. When I caught the film at its Telluride Film Festival premiere (followed by a Q&A attendees weren’t allowed to record), Fielder basically said that he and others on the filmmaking team still had trouble figuring out exactly what they’d experienced in the process of making the movie — which is a fascinating conundrum, considering that, true to its title, Holmes and her husband did let them see just about everything it seemed possible to see. My personal hunch is that Fielder came away thinking Holmes is on the level, to the extent that someone who sometimes seems like an AI program’s idea of how a human should behave can be on the level. There are a few possibilities that might explain how Holmes comes off the way she does in the movie: (a) She is a simpleton. (b) She is a conniving sociopath who happens to be utterly brilliant at playing a simpleton. (c) Somewhere between those poles, she is the very emblem of a woman who throughout her life has put herself in the sway of controlling men, to the detriment of her intellect, willpower and emotional development.

And what about those impossibly wide, unblinking eyes, and that gentle Joker smile? Are these the hallmarks, as I’ve seen theorized throughout the internet, of someone who is deeply sociopathic at worst, or on the scale at best? Or just someone with Resting Beatific Face?

The sort of feminist lens is a powerful one, if you choose to go down that path of interpretation. Fielder and Oppenheim include a moment early in the film in which Holmes’ father blurts out that he believes things really started to change for his daughter when she was raped in her college days. On-camera, Fielder offers one of the quietly startled reaction shots that are a staple of the movie, and the topic never comes up again. The theme of her becoming the victim of powerful men continues — a little bit when the subject of Theranos co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani comes up (although recounting past history doesn’t take up much of this doc’s running time), and a lot when we get to the present day. Evans is as close as “You Can See Everything” has to a villain, and probably crosses the line into counting as one. Even he is treated as a rounded human being over the course of the film; he’s too candid and open about ihs intentions to count as a top-level devil, and it seems like he might actually love Holmes. But the succession of constant revelations about what he’s up to in the last hour of the movie make Holmes feel like a woman with virtually no personal agency, even before she goes to jail, let alone afterward, when he is making deals without her knowledge and keeping up a cocky, profane tweetstorm under her name that bears scant resemblance to her personality as we know it.

It may be not giving Holmes nearly enough credit for her misdeeds to suggest that she has actually spent most of her adult years as a puppet. Yet the portrait of her passivity in the face of an aggressive “let me handle everything” man never stops growing more startling as the film goes on… and has to feel at least a little real for anyone with much first-hand human-race experience.

Two scenes that explore Holmes’ seeming — and shocking — naivete stand out. (Neither of these count as major “plot” spoilers.) One comes early on when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied, and when she says no, he asks the inevitable what-about-white-lies question. Even then, it’s a no, as Fielder almost begs her to admit that she understands the question and has told a fib or two to protect a friend’s feelings. Probably 99.99% of the population would surrender at the point — evil geniuses most of all — but Holmes can’t admit to even having falsely complimented a pal. Later on, there’s a mind-blowing scene in which Fielder uses the historically famous Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” sketch as a setup to explore how people’s communication paths might just blow right by each other. Holmes hasn’t heard of the skit, but after watching it, she says she sees what he’s trying to say… which itself turns out to be a white lie, because she finally admits that she just doesn’t get what’s going on between Abbott and Costello, at all . And it’s at this point that you might start to wonder if she is just developmentally disabled in some way.

Stunted in her growth, somehow, yet capable of convincing smart people to part with billions of dollars? Something here does not compute. And yet, intuitively, Holmes does not come off in this movie as someone with the kind of intellectual cunning to pretend not to understand an Abbott and Costello sketch that has entertained millions, or to not know what a white lie is. The enigma deepens.

But so does the possibility that, for all her sins, and for all her Stanford education, Holmes is a simple gal — not simpleton — suffering from an extreme case of not just serial male dominance but terminal Imposters’ Syndrome. (Which is something that, from the available evidence in the movie, she surely would not admit to, not least of all because she might never have heard of it.)

How people feel about Holmes after watching “You Can See Everything” might be the most divisive thing in America since… well, since Kelly Clarkson versus the Brooklyn boutique, the thing that has truly riven us as a nation. But one thing is clear: In this era of ever-shortening quick hits and hot takes, Fielder and Oppenheim’s luxuriously paced peering into someone’s soul feels like a balm, inconclusive or not. Is it possible that the more you learn about someone, the less you might know how to think about them?

To take a cue from Shakespeare: “You Can See Everything” suggests that there are more things in the heaven and earth that is just one person than are dreamt of in any of our philosophies. We could do worse than to have the possibility of sympathy thrown in amid those hours of head-scratching assessment.

(By the way, who is on first…)

On a studio soundstage, the workshop director guides pairs of participants through a series of conversational exercises designed to facilitate immersion in one another’s emotional experiences. We see, but do not fully hear, the participants speaking; Suwichakornpong cuts away before the exercises are complete. Later, on the same soundstage, the theater workshop gives way to a legal consultation. Sharing their stories with a lawyer, family members detail the bureaucratic obfuscation and stalling that have left their cases against the state unresolved. These scenes are intermittently punctuated by glimpses of the production crew, who dart in and out of frame to adjust boom mics and cameras, and of Suwichakornpong herself, who sits off to the side and watches the action unfold. Narrative may question Thailand’s ability to reckon with the residues of its traumatic past, but it ultimately attests to the resilience of ongoing individual and collective efforts to inherit this struggle in the present. The film lingers on a group lighting incense and praying together for their lost loved ones at a Buddhist shrine, a mother’s dream journal in which she writes of her dead son visiting her in her sleep, and audio recorded at a memorial gathering, chronicling the myriad forms through which memory is haltingly, but insistently, sustained."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Several short films in this year’s Doc Fortnight embodied this spirit of openness by inviting viewers into new sensory and imaginative encounters with place. In dwelling on the scant artifacts her family members took with them and the street footage she filmed upon her successive returns to Iran, Khoshnoudi conceals as much as she reveals, favoring cropped framings, elliptical narration, and long stretches of silent footage. Such gestures evoke the climate of fear and internalized censorship named in Iranian poet Ahmad Shamlou’s 1972 poem Nocturnal , which opens the film: “No one talks to anyone/ For silence is speaking/ in a thousand tongues/ We gaze upon our dead/ with a vague trace of a smile/ And we wait/ for our turn to come/ with no smile!”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet the film also revises the resignation suggested by Shamlou’s lines, gradually unearthing long histories of dissent against the Islamic regime. Later, on the same soundstage, the theater workshop gives way to a legal consultation. Sharing their stories with a lawyer, family members detail the bureaucratic obfuscation and stalling that have left their cases against the state unresolved. These scenes are intermittently punctuated by glimpses of the production crew, who dart in and out of frame to adjust boom mics and cameras, and of Suwichakornpong herself, who sits off to the side and watches the action unfold. The film invites us to question how, and if, such performances can materialize emotional or political resolution.

Narrative screened in the 2026 edition of the Museum of Modern Art’s Doc Fortnight, which ran from February 23 to March 12. Other films in the lineup were similarly defined as much by what they left out as by what was contained within them. While such work can risk becoming hermetic, overpowered by the weight of its omissions, many of the titles programmed in the festival instead opened lines of flight beyond the boundaries of a given film and back into the shared social and historical world to which they—and we—belong. Narrative may question Thailand’s ability to reckon with the residues of its traumatic past, but it ultimately attests to the resilience of ongoing individual and collective efforts to inherit this struggle in the present. The film lingers on a group lighting incense and praying together for their lost loved ones at a Buddhist shrine, a mother’s dream journal in which she writes of her dead son visiting her in her sleep, and audio recorded at a memorial gathering, chronicling the myriad forms through which memory is haltingly, but insistently, sustained.

Several short films in this year’s Doc Fortnight embodied this spirit of openness by inviting viewers into new sensory and imaginative encounters with place. Tulapop Saenjaroen’s Local Sensations (2025) uses Thai architecture scholar Chatri Prakitnonthakan’s essay “How to Design a Modern Monument That Won’t Become a Shrine” as a playful point of departure to explore different ways of inhabiting space; the director restlessly recombines footage of an improvised musical performance, a glassblowing workshop, a walk through a nature center, and a drawing game amongst architecture students. Mark Jenkin’s Enough to Fill Up an Eggcup (2016) and Rhea Storr’s Okay Keskidee! Let Me See Inside (2025) similarly utilize the expressive capacities of analog film—its lush sensitivity to light, texture, and color—to attune viewers to overlooked and vulnerable landscapes. For Jenkin, it’s a Cornish fishing village whose seaside landscapes and livelihoods are increasingly threatened by rising sea levels and intensifying storms. For Storr, it’s the site of the former Keskidee Centre, a hub of Caribbean diasporic organizing and cultural production in the U.K. in the 1970s and ’80s that is now the site of a luxury apartment development. Unable to go inside, Storr’s film instead meditates on imaginative possibilities of “surface” itself through light leaks, patterns left by chemical emulsion, kaleidoscopic refractions, and optically printed text overlaying quotidian footage of diasporic neighborhoods.

Ross McElwee’s Remake (2025) is an aching reflection on the director’s relationship with his son Adrian—which was often mediated by filmmaking—and the events leading up to Adrian’s death in 2016 from a drug overdose. Narrated primarily as an address to Adrian, the film organizes these reflections along a timeline that also retraces the failed attempt by L.A. producers to develop McElwee’s personal documentary Sherman’s March (1985) into a narrative feature. “I used to call myself a filmmaker. I used to call myself your father,” McElwee states via voiceover, naming a life doubly undone by loss. In what form might such a shattered self be remade?

Perhaps, Remake suggests, in the eyes of a viewer. Over the course of the film, McElwee revisits not only his own footage but also the footage Adrian shot over his short life. The elder McElwee’s attempt to view the world through his son’s eyes occasions his most anguished reflections on all that his own camera failed to see, but the resulting work is a tender tribute to the complexity and vitality of Adrian’s relationship to the world around him. Near the end of the film, McElwee worries that such endless looking will make his son “seem like a fictional character—someone who never existed, except on film.” However, if cinema is not a substitute for life, it is, for both McElwee and Adrian, a conduit to it—a way of encountering oneself, and one another.

Bani Khoshnoudi’s The Vanishing Point (2025) also excavates a painful family history—the story of her mother’s cousin Nasanine, who was arrested and executed in Iran in 1988 during Ayatollah Khomeini’s bloody wave of political purges. After her death, Nasanine’s parents were met by prison officials with a plastic bag containing a few scattered belongings and “a threat to be silent.” The film traces the reverberations of such enforced forgetting, weaving together Nasanine’s story with Khoshnoudi and her family’s own fractured memories of exile from Iran after the revolution. In dwelling on the scant artifacts her family members took with them and the street footage she filmed upon her successive returns to Iran, Khoshnoudi conceals as much as she reveals, favoring cropped framings, elliptical narration, and long stretches of silent footage. Such gestures evoke the climate of fear and internalized censorship named in Iranian poet Ahmad Shamlou’s 1972 poem Nocturnal , which opens the film: “No one talks to anyone/ For silence is speaking/ in a thousand tongues/ We gaze upon our dead/ with a vague trace of a smile/ And we wait/ for our turn to come/ with no smile!”

Yet the film also revises the resignation suggested by Shamlou’s lines, gradually unearthing long histories of dissent against the Islamic regime. After a montage of video and cell-phone footage documenting mass protests in Iran, the film ends with a haunting audio recording from 2023 of women singing together in Evin prison, echoing earlier footage in which families of those disappeared by the regime gather and sing in protest around a mass grave. Shamlou’s thousand-tongued silence gives way to a thousand-tongued voice of defiance, emblematic of the film’s broader shift from a personal reflection on absence to a collective history of action.

The Vanishing Point held its U.S. premiere mere days after the U.S. and Israel jointly initiated war on Iran, cynically appropriating Iranian dissent to sanction the brutal extension of their military agendas. Watching the film, I thought about the Iranians reporting on the destruction of their homes amidst a near-total internet blackout. I thought, too, of the crowds in Los Angeles and Minneapolis facing down ICE abductions, and those presently taking to the streets to demand an end to our forever wars abroad. Their astonishing bravery in confronting authoritarian violence reverberates across our ever-expanding archive of footage documented via phones and cameras, but their demand exceeds the boundaries of these frames. They push us not merely to watch our screens, but to fight for the world beyond them.

article_text:
Two-time Oscar-nominated producer Rodrigo Teixeira will receive the inaugural Árbol de la Vida Visionary Award at the GuadaLAjara Film Festival (GLAFF), the Los Angeles offshoot of the Guadalajara International Film Festival, on Nov. 6.

The honor will be presented by Oscar-nominated actor Wagner Moura ahead of a screening of James Gray’s “ Paper Tiger ,” which Teixeira produced. The award recognizes individuals who have made a lasting impact on cinema and strengthened the ties between Latin America and the international film industry.

Teixeira will also serve as the first mentor of the GLAFF Co-Production Lab, a new industry initiative developed with the Guadalajara International Film Festival (FICG) to foster co-productions between Mexico and the United States.

“Rodrigo Teixeira has built a career defined by bold storytelling and a true commitment to artists across the border,” says Ximena Urrutia, executive director of GLAFF. “As inaugural mentor of our New Mexico-U. S. co-production lab, he will help emerging filmmakers turn ambitious cross-border projects into lasting partnerships.”

For more than two decades, Teixeira has bridged Latin American and global filmmaking through his production company RT Features, whose credits include “Call Me by Your Name,” “The Lighthouse,” “The Witch” and “Invisible Life.” He earned best picture nominations for “Call Me by Your Name” and Walter Salles’ “I’m Still Here,” which won the Oscar for international feature. Films from his banner have collected nine Oscar nominations and six Golden Globe nominations.

“Paper Tiger” marks the third collaboration between Teixeira and Gray, following “Ad Astra” and “Armageddon Time.”

The 16th edition of GLAFF runs Nov. 5-7 in Los Angeles, opening with Diego Luna’s “Ashes” and closing with Eddie Sánchez’s “Mexicanamerican.”

article_text:
From 30 October 30, Galerie Écho 119 in Paris presents “à marée basse” (at low tide) , a new exhibition conceived with and by the curator Sonia Voss .

This journey into the depths of the ocean will be explored through the lens of photographer Kusukazu Uraguchi (1922–1988), who spent nearly thirty years photographing the ama (the Japanese women who free-drive) of his region, and French ceramicist Laure Gilquin (b. 1981), whose work draws inspiration from the forms and materials of the underwater world.

For over three thousand years, the ama – Japan’s ‘women of the sea’ – have inhabited the archipelago’s shores, free-diving in search of seaweed and abalone. Their sensual connection to the water, their fearlessness and their self-assurance have, over the centuries, fascinated poets and artists.

The Japanese photographer Kusukazu Uraguchi (1922–1988), originally from Shima (Mie Prefecture), devoted more than thirty years capturing the lives of the ama in his region. His photographs shed light on their age-old practices which were already under threat of disappearing at the time whilst capturing their energy in every moment. The exhibition draws on Uraguchi’s archive, which contains tens of thousands of negatives and had long remained unexplored.

Sonia Voss , Exhibition Curator

Kusukazu Uraguchi was born in 1922 in Fuseda, Shima. After the war, he worked as a pearl merchant before turning his hand to photography; his early career was marked by the publication of a photograph in Camera Mainichi in 1956. From 1972 onwards, his photographs appeared regularly in several Japanese magazines and were exhibited throughout Japan. He published Shima Fudoki in 1978, followed by Shima no ama in 1982, both books devoted to his native region. He died of pneumonia in 1988.

His work was brought back to the public’s attention at the Rencontres d’Arles 2024 thanks to the efforts of curator Sonia Voss.

The exhibition will be followed by a presentation at Paris Photo (12–15 November) featuring a display on the theme of ‘female divers’, again showcasing the work of Kusukazu Uraguchi , alongside that of artist-researcher Laure Winants and Japanese photographer Kazuo Kitai .

article_text:
Films and events

Debate

Amazomania

This reframing of ‘adventure journalist’ Erling Söderström’s 1996 Amazonian expedition to the isolated Korubo people is an unflinching critique of the ethics of first-contact filmmaking.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Nathan Grossman

Screenwriters Jordana Berg, Olof Berglind

Sweden-Denmark-France 2026. 93min

Courtesy of Autlook Filmsales

Languages Portuguese, French, English, Swedish, Korubo With English subtitles

Introduction

Digging into the Swedish journalist’s unreleased archives, documentarian Nathan Grossman flips a ‘White Saviour’ narrative on its head by juxtaposing extraordinary but deeply uncomfortable original footage with an alarming 2023 reunion, in which the Korubo finally get to speak for themselves. Amazomania is a fierce deconstruction of the camera’s gaze and a reckoning on who really owns Indigenous stories.

Sarah Lutton

With thanks to Embassy of Sweden.

Content advice

Contains scenes of animal slaughter.

Contains racist attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Rebellion

Revolution is the beat that drums through this electrifying story about the landmark case against the Bradford 12.

Tropical Fractals

Leonardo Pirondi’s timely reflection on ecological collapse imagines a future in which a biodome spaceship preserves the last traces of life on Earth.

Concrete Land

Asmahan Bkerat’s feature directorial debut is an intimate, multi-generational portrait of a mixed-raced family fighting displacement and hostility in Jordan.

article_text:
In a major shift in the theatrical tides, Netflix has reported box office grosses for the first time ever.

The streamer’s awards hopeful “ La Bola Negra ” scored $277,500 from just four theaters, averaging $69,375 per location. Those ticket sales are notable as the second-highest screen average ever for a non-English language film behind 2019’s “Parasite,” which opened to $393,216 from three theaters, averaging $131,072 per location. It’s also the highest-ever PSA — the key metric for arthouse releases — for a Spanish language film. By comparison, Neon’s multilingual legal thriller “Fjord,” another Oscar contender, debuted last weekend to $124,000 from four theaters, translating to $31,000 per location.

Now the test is whether “La Bola Negra” can sustain momentum as Netflix slowly expands the movie’s footprint in the weeks to come. The streamer plans to keep the film in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times and the company’s longest theatrical rollout to date, before its Netflix release on Dec. 2. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known as Los Javis, “La Bola Negra” is a generation-spanning queer epic that chronicles the interconnected story of three men. After the drama was embraced at Cannes Film Festival with a 16-minute standing ovation , Netflix acquired the movie for around $5 million. “La Bola Negra” tied for the Cannes best director prize and won Toronto Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award, which has historically been a reliable indicator of Academy Awards attention.

Popular on Variety

Netflix has long been viewed as a major big-screen adversary, probably because the company’s co-CEO Ted Sarandos has frequently dismissed movie theaters as an “outmoded idea.” And while the streamer has been warming to theaters beyond just Oscar-qualifying runs, with token releases for 2022’s “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Story” and last year’s”Kpop Demon Hunters” re-release and the “Stranger Things” series finale , Netflix has never disclosed how much those movies made in cinemas.

In the past, Netflix has viewed multiplexes, not as a financial strategy, but rather as a marketing stunt to drive interest pack to the platform. But there are other benefits to box office reporting for Netflix, which has never won the coveted best picture Oscar. Unlike streaming metrics, which can be twisted and touted in any which way, box office dollars are uniformly reported — meaning there’s no denying a hit (or a miss). Netflix’s change in strategy comes as the streamer’s stock has been languishing. Last week, the company laid off 1,000 employees and replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Disney veteran Peter Rice.

Moving forward, Netflix plans to disclose grosses for upcoming releases such as David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” around Thanksgiving and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and Taika Waititi’s animated “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory” in 2027. Whether those buzzy projects achieve breakout status, Netflix’s new attention toward theatrical is a win for exhibitors, who are already celebrating the biggest post-COVID year at the box office.

article_text:
The cast of “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” brought the glow of a Hollywood standing ovation to the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival on Sunday, two days before Yamazaki Takashi’s follow-up to his Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One” opens in Japan.

Kamiki Ryunosuke, who returns as lead character Shikishima Koichi, and Hamabe Minami, who reprises the role of his wife Noriko, had flown back to Japan only two days earlier from the film’s premiere at Los Angeles’ TCL Chinese Theatre.

“The energy was simply extraordinary,” Kamiki said. “Feeling that raw enthusiasm firsthand made me realize all over again just how deeply Godzilla is loved around the world. It was an invaluable experience.”

Applause in the 900-seat theater reportedly ran on without a break. Hamabe said the cast later met premiere-goers at an after-party, where many approached them with big smiles to share their reactions. Some had dressed in Godzilla-themed outfits or wore Godzilla badges.

The red carpet was open to passersby, Kamiki recalled. Some fans held up large posters and asked for autographs, while chants of the director’s first name broke out from the crowd. “It wasn’t just a polite ‘Takashi,’” he said. “It was like: ‘TAKASHI! HEY, TAKASHI!’ It was roaring.” When Yamazaki went over to sign autographs, the crowd erupted again, leaving Kamiki convinced that “Takashi of the world is truly amazing.”

The Tokyo event also marked the first stage appearance of child actor Nagatani Sae, who returns as Shikishima Akiko. Kamiki walked her onstage.

In “Minus One,” which aired on Japanese TV’s “Friday Roadshow” on Friday, Akiko’s part consisted mostly of crying or single words such as “Where?” This time, the script gave her full dialogue. “We were like, ‘Really? Can she do this?’” Kamiki said. “But when we got on set, she had all her lines memorized perfectly and delivered them flawlessly.”

Hamabe said Nagatani had barely left toddlerhood during the first shoot and was easily frightened by the many adults on set. “So reuniting on this film, I was amazed by how much of a wonderful young girl she had grown into,” she said. “She chatted with us so much, taught me various things, and was very dependable in her acting.”

Nagatani said she wasn’t nervous during filming. She recalled Kamiki continuing to rub her back even after the cut was called on a scene in which Akiko cries. She then asked her co-stars how she could become a fine actor while still in elementary school. Kamiki told her she already outshone them both, and said that appearing in both “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” at her age was “an amazing achievement in itself.”

According to Kamiki, the new film picks up two years after the events of “Minus One.” “I hope viewers can imagine what those two years were like for them, and see how the family stands together against what comes next,” he said. Hamabe put the gap at two to three years. She said the family had settled into everyday life together before Godzilla resurfaces to threaten it.

Asked why the franchise has endured, Kamiki echoed the view of the director and fellow cast members that each Godzilla film mirrors the era in which it is made. “But personally, when I reflect on it, take Godzilla’s existence or the theme music: I cannot even remember when I first heard it or realized, ‘Oh, this is Godzilla’s theme song,’” he said. “It has always been alongside us, which is why I personally think it has remained loved for so long.”

Hamabe said that from a human standpoint, Godzilla is overwhelming and impossible to defeat. “Yet, when Godzilla appears, humans unite and stand together to face it,” she said. “I think seeing that human resolve is the first thing that moves people’s hearts.”

“Minus One,” the 30th Japanese live-action entry in the Godzilla franchise, grossed more than JPY7.65 billion ($50 million) at the local box office. It became the first Asian production to take home the visual effects prize at the 96th Oscars, and went on to collect more than 50 honors at home and abroad.

“Minus Zero” is the first Japanese film to be certified as Filmed for Imax.

article_text:
Pocket Review

A Little Fantasy Goes a Long Way

In this photography exhibition, works vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show.

Hyperallergic )

“Abandon the search for Truth; settle for a good fantasy.” These words, taken from Fran Lebowitz and written on the wall to warn all ye who enter Luhring Augustine’s Chelsea gallery, set up the premise for its current group show: settle for a good fantasy .

It’s an admittedly juicy quotation. So juicy, indeed, that the gallery has hung Shaun Pierson’s photograph of a very voluptuous strawberry — seriously, it’s like the Venus of Willendorf of strawberries — right next to it, as if to underscore the point: Photography is always chasing a fantasy.

The exhibition’s main room leans into this, showing portraiture's fragmentary, erotic side. Works by Pierson, David Seidner, and Janice Guy vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show. Curved, freckled backs touch. Beautiful shards of women’s faces are pieced together, seemingly pulled from the dark. Guy’s grids of self-portraits from the 1970s are particularly arresting, and not just because she also happens to be beautiful.
